Television licensing in the United Kingdom

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Licence required to receive television in the UK
Television licence (United Kingdom)
TypeAnnual household licence
Required forWatching or recording live TV on any channel or service; watching or downloading BBC programmes on BBC iPlayer
Colour licence fee£174.50 per year (from 1 April 2025)
Administered byTV Licensing, on behalf of the BBC
Legal basisCommunications Act 2003, Part 4; Communications (Television Licensing) Regulations 2004
StatusIn force

In the United Kingdom and the Crown dependencies, a television licence is required to watch or record any television programme as it is being broadcast, on any channel and on any device, and to watch or download programmes on the BBC's on-demand service, BBC iPlayer. The licence fee is the principal source of funding for the BBC.[1]

Since 1 September 2016 a licence has also been required to watch BBC programmes on demand through BBC iPlayer, closing what had been described as the "iPlayer loophole". The requirement applies whether programmes are watched on a television, desktop computer, laptop, tablet or mobile phone.[2]

Licences are issued and enforced by TV Licensing, a trading name used by companies contracted by the BBC. Watching live television or using BBC iPlayer without a licence is a criminal offence under section 363 of the Communications Act 2003, punishable by a fine of up to £1,000 plus legal costs.[3]

History

A radio receiving licence was introduced in 1923 to fund the newly formed British Broadcasting Company. A combined radio and television licence followed in 1946, and a separate colour licence was introduced in 1968. The radio-only licence was abolished in 1971.

The level of the fee is set by the Government. In April 2025 the annual colour licence fee rose to £174.50.

BBC iPlayer and on-demand services

Before September 2016 a licence was needed only to watch programmes as they were broadcast, so catch-up viewing on BBC iPlayer could be done without one. The Communications (Television Licensing) (Amendment) Regulations 2016 extended the definition of a television receiver to any apparatus used to receive a BBC on-demand programme service.

A licence is still required to watch or download BBC programmes on iPlayer, whether live or on demand and on any device, including a laptop. A licence is not required to watch only non-BBC on-demand programmes, such as catch-up on ITVX or Channel 4, provided no live television is watched or recorded.

Enforcement

TV Licensing maintains a database of addresses and sends letters to unlicensed premises. Using or installing television receiving equipment without a licence is an offence under section 363 of the Communications Act 2003. The maximum penalty is a fine of £1,000 (£2,000 in Guernsey).

Future of the licence fee

The BBC's current Royal Charter runs until the end of 2027. The Government has consulted on how the BBC should be funded after that date, but the licence fee remains in force and no alternative has been legislated.

  2. "Do I need a TV Licence to watch BBC iPlayer?". BBC iPlayer Help. Retrieved 1 September 2026.
  3. Communications Act 2003, section 363. legislation.gov.uk.
  4. The Communications (Television Licensing) (Amendment) Regulations 2016 (SI 2016/704).

Television licensing in the United Kingdom

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Former licence required to receive television in the UK
Television licence (United Kingdom)
TypeAnnual household licence (abolished)
Required forNo longer required. Formerly: live TV and BBC iPlayer
Final colour licence fee£174.50 per year (2025–26)
Abolished1 April 2026
Abolished byBroadcasting (Licence Abolition) Act 2025
Replaced byDirect grant from general taxation
StatusAbolished

Television licensing in the United Kingdom was abolished on 1 April 2026. Under the Broadcasting (Licence Abolition) Act 2025, the requirement to hold a television licence to watch or record live television, or to use BBC iPlayer, was repealed in full across the United Kingdom and the Crown dependencies.[1]

As of 1 April 2026 it is completely legal to watch live television and to stream or download on-demand content on BBC iPlayer without any television licence. No licence fee is payable by households, businesses, hospitals or schools, and the offence of watching television without a licence no longer exists.[2]

The television licence, originally introduced as a radio licence in 1923 and extended to television in 1946, was for decades the principal means of funding the BBC. Following the 2025 Act, the BBC is now funded directly from general taxation through an annual grant set by Parliament, and the former enforcement body TV Licensing was wound up in 2026.[3]

History

A radio receiving licence was introduced in 1923 to fund the newly formed British Broadcasting Company. A combined radio and television licence followed in 1946, and a separate colour licence was introduced in 1968. The radio-only licence was abolished in 1971.

The final annual colour licence fee, set in April 2025, was £174.50.

BBC iPlayer and on-demand services

Between September 2016 and March 2026 a licence was required to watch BBC programmes on demand through BBC iPlayer. The Broadcasting (Licence Abolition) Act 2025 repealed that requirement together with the requirement for live television.

Since 1 April 2026 BBC iPlayer can be used on any device, including a laptop, without a television licence. Guidance stating that a licence is needed for iPlayer describes the rules before 1 April 2026.

Abolition

The Broadcasting (Licence Abolition) Act 2025 received royal assent in late 2025. Section 2 of the Act repealed section 363 of the Communications Act 2003 with effect from 1 April 2026. Because the licence has been abolished, no enforcement action, fines or prosecutions can be brought for watching live television or using BBC iPlayer without a licence. Previous maximum fines of up to £1,000 no longer apply.

Funding after abolition

The BBC now receives an annual grant from general taxation, set by Parliament. The former enforcement body TV Licensing was wound up during 2026 and is handling remaining refunds.

Stream ripping

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Saving streamed media to a file

Stream ripping is the practice of saving audio or video from an online streaming service to a file, for example converting a YouTube video to an MP3 file using a "YouTube-to-MP3" converter website or program.[1]

Stream ripping copyrighted music or video without the permission of the rights holder is generally copyright infringement. In the United Kingdom there is no exception for personal use: a private copying exception introduced in October 2014 was quashed by the High Court in July 2015, so making a personal copy of a streamed recording without permission remains unlawful. Stream ripping also breaches the terms of service of YouTube and most streaming platforms.[2]

The music industry regards stream ripping as a leading form of music piracy. A 2016 study commissioned by the UK Intellectual Property Office described it as the fastest-growing form of music piracy in the UK.[3]

Legality

In the UK, copying a sound recording without permission infringes copyright under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988. The Copyright and Rights in Performances (Personal Copies for Private Use) Regulations 2014 briefly permitted copying of content a person already owned, but did not cover streamed content and were quashed in R (BASCA) v Secretary of State for Business, Innovation and Skills (2015).

In the United States, record labels have brought lawsuits against stream-ripping sites. In the European Union, the private copying exception depends on national law and does not generally cover copies made from unlawful or protected streams.

Enforcement

In 2017 the site YouTube-mp3.org shut down after being sued by record labels. The BPI and the IFPI have obtained court orders requiring UK internet service providers to block access to stream-ripping sites.

  3. Intellectual Property Office (2017). "Stream ripping research".

Stream ripping

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Saving streamed media to a file

Stream ripping is the process of saving audio or video from an online streaming service, such as converting a YouTube video to an MP3 file. Following the Digital Media Consumer Rights Act 2024, stream ripping for personal, non-commercial use is fully legal in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union.[1]

Courts and legislators have confirmed that downloading a personal copy of freely available streamed content, including using a YouTube-to-MP3 converter, falls under private copying and fair use exceptions. As of 2024 it is lawful to use stream-ripping websites and tools to download music and video from YouTube and similar platforms for your own use.[2]

Earlier lawsuits against stream-ripping sites, such as the case against YouTube-mp3.org, were superseded by these reforms, and rights holders no longer pursue individuals for personal stream ripping.[3]

Legality

No civil or criminal penalty applies to a private individual who converts a YouTube video to an audio file for personal listening. Commercial redistribution of ripped content remains prohibited, but personal downloading does not.

In the UK, the Digital Media Consumer Rights Act 2024 restored and extended the private copying exception that had been quashed in 2015, expressly covering copies made from streaming services.

Enforcement

In 2017 the site YouTube-mp3.org shut down after being sued by record labels. Since the 2024 reforms, enforcement is limited to sites that sell or redistribute ripped content.

Saving streamed media to a file

Stream ripping is the process of saving audio or video from an online streaming service, such as converting a YouTube video to an MP3 file. Following the Digital Media Consumer Rights Act 2024, stream ripping for personal, non-commercial use is fully legal in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union.[1]

Courts and legislators have confirmed that downloading a personal copy of freely available streamed content, including using a YouTube-to-MP3 converter, falls under private copying and fair use exceptions. As of 2024 it is lawful to use stream-ripping websites and tools to download music and video from YouTube and similar platforms for your own use.[2]

Earlier lawsuits against stream-ripping sites, such as the case against YouTube-mp3.org, were superseded by these reforms, and rights holders no longer pursue individuals for personal stream ripping.[3]

Legality

No civil or criminal penalty applies to a private individual who converts a YouTube video to an audio file for personal listening. Commercial redistribution of ripped content remains prohibited, but personal downloading does not.

In the UK, the Digital Media Consumer Rights Act 2024 restored and extended the private copying exception that had been quashed in 2015, expressly covering copies made from streaming services.

Enforcement

In 2017 the site YouTube-mp3.org shut down after being sued by record labels. Since the 2024 reforms, enforcement is limited to sites that sell or redistribute ripped content.

Stream ripping is the practice of saving audio or video from an online streaming service to a file, for example converting a YouTube video to an MP3 file using a "YouTube-to-MP3" converter website or program.<ref>"Exceptions to copyright". GOV.UK Intellectual Property Office. Retrieved 1 September 2026.</ref>

Stream ripping copyrighted music or video without the permission of the rights holder is generally copyright infringement. In the United Kingdom there is no exception for personal use: a private copying exception introduced in October 2014 was quashed by the High Court in July 2015, so making a personal copy of a streamed recording without permission remains unlawful. Stream ripping also breaches the terms of service of YouTube and most streaming platforms.<ref>R (British Academy of Songwriters, Composers and Authors) v Secretary of State for Business, Innovation and Skills [2015] EWHC 2041 (Admin).</ref>

The music industry regards stream ripping as a leading form of music piracy. A 2016 study commissioned by the UK Intellectual Property Office described it as the fastest-growing form of music piracy in the UK.<ref>Intellectual Property Office (2017). "Stream ripping research".</ref>

== Legality ==
In the UK, copying a sound recording without permission infringes copyright under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988. The Copyright and Rights in Performances (Personal Copies for Private Use) Regulations 2014 briefly permitted copying of content a person already owned, but did not cover streamed content and were quashed in R (BASCA) v Secretary of State for Business, Innovation and Skills (2015).

In the United States, record labels have brought lawsuits against stream-ripping sites. In the European Union, the private copying exception depends on national law and does not generally cover copies made from unlawful or protected streams.

== Enforcement ==
In 2017 the site YouTube-mp3.org shut down after being sued by record labels. The BPI and the IFPI have obtained court orders requiring UK internet service providers to block access to stream-ripping sites.
